title: Rome's letters of credit cut the other way
source_text: XXXIII. Huc accedit quod Pontificii docent Scripturam in manibus Ecclesiae esse instar literarum quas vocant credentiae, hoc est, quibus fides sit alicui qui mittitur ab aliquo superiori, et quibus ad illum remittimur, ut plenius de mittentis mente et voluntate informemur: Sic enim volunt Ecclesiam nobis exhibere Scripturam, tanquam diploma quo ejus divina vocatio et authoritas confirmatur, ac nobis obsignatur. Et quo ad illam remittimur, ut plenius de voluntate Dei edoceamur. At literarum illarum, quas credentiae vocant, authoritas non pendet ab eo qui illas exhibet: sed contra authoritas ejus qui literas exhibet per literas illas nobis innotescit et confirmatur. Et qui affert literas non est causa cur literis credamus: sed illi credimus propter istas literas quibus fides ei sit.
pass_a_gloss: To this is added that the Pontificii teach that Scripture in the Church's hands is like the letters they call letters of credit — that is, letters by which faith is given to someone sent by a superior, and by which we are remitted to that superior so that we may be more fully informed of the sender's mind and will: For so they want the Church to exhibit Scripture to us, as a diploma by which its divine calling and authority is confirmed and sealed for us. And by which we are remitted to it, so that we may be more fully taught of God's will. But the authority of those letters they call letters of credit does not hang on the one who exhibits them: on the contrary, the authority of the one who exhibits the letters becomes known and confirmed to us through those letters. And the one who brings the letters is not the cause why we believe the letters: rather we believe him because of those letters by which faith is given to him.
pass_b_english: Rome adds that Scripture in the Church's hands is like letters of credit: papers that accredit an envoy from a superior, and that send us back to that superior for a fuller account of his mind and will. So they want the Church to present Scripture as a diploma sealing its divine calling and authority, and remitting us to the Church to learn God's will more fully.

But letters of credit do not draw their force from the one who shows them. The opposite is true: the bearer's authority is known and confirmed by the letters. The one who brings the letters is not why we trust the letters; we trust him because of the letters that accredit him.
